title: Getting Off with the Luddites | Sarah Thankam Mathews
gist: A first-person report from inside New York's neo-Luddite scene: a leaderless network of newsletters (NYC Off Tech), anonymous artist-activists, the School of Radical Attention, and dumbphone companies like dumb.co and Lightphone, whose theory of change is free unadvertised public events rather than antitrust lobbying. Their real target is data and its fusion with the state — AI framed as 'a gigantic intensification of data power' — and the movement's most investable insight is Damian Thomas's argument that platform lock-in is a producer problem, not a consumer one, alongside hard numbers on screen capture and Gallup finding seven in ten Americans oppose a local AI data center.

themes.theme: Anatomy of the NYC neo-Luddite scene

insights.claim: New York has developed an organized neo-Luddite network that formed over the last couple of years around divesting from Big Tech, spending less time online and connecting in person, extending well beyond the Gen-Z phoneless-party trend pieces that describe it.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: An organized cultural constituency against consumer tech is forming in the media capital, which is where narrative-driven regulatory pressure typically originates.
insights.locator: Then in the fall a couple people mentioned New York City’s “neo-Luddite scene”

insights.claim: The scene includes commercial players selling minimalist devices and digital-detox offerings — specifically dumb.co and Lightphone — for people who want to stay connected without the addictive ecosystems of Big Tech.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Identifies a real if small revenue surface — deliberately degraded hardware as a paid product category with an organized cultural movement doing free marketing for it.
insights.locator: There are people affiliated with companies like dumb.co and Lightphone

insights.claim: The intellectual and media infrastructure of the movement already exists, spanning the School of Radical Attention founded by Princeton graduates for attention activism, Brian Merchant's Blood in the Machine, Edward Ongweso Jr.'s Substack The Tech Bubble, and TikTok/Instagram influencer Adam Aleksic with a millions-strong following as @etymologynerd.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Anti-tech sentiment now has distribution through the same platforms it opposes, which accelerates how fast the narrative can scale.
insights.locator: There are writers and thinkers like Brian Merchant

insights.claim: The artist-activist wing operates anonymously under pseudonyms like Captain Ludd and General Ludd and sends a puppet spokesperson named Gowanus to media appearances, with Hasan Minhaj having already interviewed the puppet and Chelsea Handler trying.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: A media strategy that builds a recognizable brand without identifiable leaders is resistant to the personality-attack playbook usually used to defuse tech-critical movements.
insights.locator: To aid them in this mission, they’d created a spokes-puppet named Gowanus

insights.claim: Turnout observed across events ranged from about ninety people at a Midtown panel to hundreds circling the Fifth Avenue Apple store to roughly four hundred at the Summer of Ludd opening play — real but small scale relative to what the movement opposes.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Calibrates the movement's current size: culturally potent, commercially negligible today — the signal is trajectory, not present scale.
insights.locator: When I arrived, I found about ninety people

insights.claim: The movement's explicit theory of change, laid out in a zine titled The Event Is The Medium, is free public participatory events with no tickets, no social-media invitation, no closed guest list and no promise of going to plan, in the hope others replicate the format.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Deliberate refusal of digital distribution makes the movement invisible to social-listening tools — sentiment monitoring will systematically undercount it.
insights.locator: Back at S.H.I.T.P.H.O.N.E, someone had handed me a zine

insights.claim: Summer of Ludd, a weeklong festival of more than 120 free public events in Tompkins Square Park starting at the end of June, was publicized entirely through wheatpasting, flyering and a phone hotline rather than social media, as a deliberate structure test of whether a mass event can be mobilized offline.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: If offline-only mobilization works at this scale, it demonstrates that platform distribution is not a prerequisite for cultural reach — a direct challenge to the platforms' core value proposition.
insights.locator: Apropos of this, they told me about “Summer of Ludd,”

insights.claim: These Luddites make few direct demands of institutional power, with no antitrust lobbying and no push to regulate addictive design or remove ed tech from schools, though a couple volunteered for New York congressional candidate Alex Bores and some tracked Jonathan Haidt's work on adolescent smartphone use.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Near-term regulatory risk to platforms from this specific movement is low; the risk it creates is slower-moving cultural and norm change.
insights.locator: The Luddites I spoke to made few direct demands

insights.claim: Unlike the original Luddites, the contemporary movement does not advocate property destruction beyond symbolic acts such as ceremonially smashing an iPad with a hammer at a rally.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Rules out the sabotage tail risk that the Luddite label implies — the movement is a reputational and cultural actor, not a physical-security one.
insights.locator: Unlike their forebears, these Luddites did not advocate

insights.claim: The stated aim is to undo decades of social conditioning by technology and reorient people toward unmediated embodied connection one in-person meet-up at a time, inspiring people to make tech work for them rather than the reverse.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The success metric to watch is norm change (phone use in social settings), not membership counts or policy wins.
insights.locator: The aim was lofty: to undo decades of social conditioning

themes.theme: Data, not technology, as the enemy

insights.claim: The movement's precise target is not technology but data — its collection, quantification and transformation of human beings into measurable, sortable, governable units — and its growing fusion with the state.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Reframes the political attack surface from screen time onto data collection and government partnerships, which is where the real regulatory exposure for platforms sits.
insights.quote: Data was a machinery of legibility, and legibility was often the precondition for control.
insights.locator: The menace, to them, was more specific than “technology,”

insights.claim: Organizers frame AI not as a malevolent superintelligence but as a gigantic intensification of data power, deliberately rejecting the existential-risk framing that dominates elite AI discourse.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: A left-coded AI critique centered on surveillance rather than doom would attack different targets — data brokerage, government contracts, biometric systems — than the AI-safety lobby does.
insights.quote: AI was not, to them, a malevolent superintelligence so much as a gigantic intensification of data power.
insights.locator: AI was not, to them, a malevolent superintelligence

insights.claim: The operative distinction organizers use is between a tool that helps with life and an infrastructure that captures life, which is what lets technologists themselves participate in an anti-Big-Tech movement.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: A test that condemns platform business models while sparing hardware and self-hosted software — useful for predicting which products this constituency will accept.
insights.quote: Gowanus made a distinction between a tool that helped with life and an infrastructure that captured life
insights.locator: Gowanus made a distinction between a tool

insights.claim: Organizers ground their opposition in the historical claim that fascist systems require populations to be classified before they can be ranked, targeted, excluded, deported or disappeared, citing Cambridge Analytica's role in Trumpism and IBM's collusion with the Nazis.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: This is the argument that converts privacy from a consumer preference into a civil-liberties emergency — the frame most likely to mobilize broad political coalitions against data infrastructure.
insights.locator: Captain Ludd referenced Cambridge Analytica’s role

insights.claim: Membership is deliberately non-exclusive: you can be a Luddite and own a smartphone, though most core organizers choose not to, and the group emphasizes freedom to set one's own relationship to tools and inconvenience.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: A low barrier to entry is what would let this scale into mass politics rather than remaining a subculture — the key variable for whether it ever affects platform revenue.
insights.locator: As far as many neo-Luddites were concerned

themes.theme: Platform lock-in is a producer problem

insights.claim: Damian Thomas argues people stay on platforms that make them actively unhappy because their friends, shows, events, political updates, artists and creative communities were all pushed there — making it a producer problem, not a consumer problem, so the organizing target is producers.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The sharpest structural read on platform moats in the piece: user churn is blocked by supply-side presence, so any credible platform disruption must move creators first.
insights.quote: that is a producer problem. And that’s why I’m trying to organize those producers.
insights.locator: People, in his eyes, were staying on platforms

insights.claim: Thomas built Unplatform in January 2025 as an interactive guide to help people leave social media, found it hard to get anyone to actually quit, and pivoted to rebuilding the discovery infrastructure platforms displaced.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that consumer-side detox tools fail on their own — the durable opportunity is substitute infrastructure, not exit assistance.
insights.locator: In January 2025, he built Unplatform

insights.claim: Big Tech's success wiped out the old architecture of independent culture — alt weeklies, local papers, record stores, bulletin boards, magazines, event calendars and small subculture publications — leaving no non-platform answer to the question 'What's happening?'
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Names the specific vacated market: local discovery and event listings, the layer aggregators monetized and degraded, now open to lower-tech re-entrants.
insights.locator: Now he lamented how much Big Tech had succeeded

insights.claim: The proposed replacement is a combination of offline and 'Web 1.5' lower-tech alternatives so that musicians, writers, artists, organizers and venues can stop trying to play the algorithm like Vegas slots.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Points at demand for deliberately un-algorithmic distribution tools — newsletters, calendars, directories — as a niche with committed early adopters.
insights.locator: Thomas began to shift his focus toward rebuilding

insights.claim: Thomas expects no meaningful US federal action on tech issues any time soon and argues politics flows downstream of culture, so grassroots organizational capacity should be built first and leveraged to pressure Congress later.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: An informed activist's own base case is that near-term regulatory risk to platforms is low — useful as a counterweight to headline antitrust noise.
insights.quote: The enclosure of culture is happening right now. There’s an immediacy,
insights.locator: “I don’t think that the US federal government is going to produce

themes.theme: Screen capture, willpower and synthetic intimacy

insights.claim: Nick Plante, who studied the social and developmental effects of social media and smartphones at UPenn, found that people undervalue situational factors like groupthink and cultural norms in device use and overestimate their own willpower, assuming they would recognize and be able to quit a problem.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Explains why individual detox products underperform and why norm-level interventions (school bans, group settings) move usage more than willpower-based ones.
insights.locator: He saw evidence that people undervalued situational factors

insights.claim: The global average TikTok user watches over 100,000 videos annually, the average American spends 50 hours a week on screens including 16 on social media platforms, and an American born in 2025 is projected to spend 21 years of their lifetime looking at screens.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The attention base these platforms monetize is enormous and still growing, which is exactly why a norm shift of even a few percentage points would be materially visible in engagement metrics.
insights.locator: I learned that the global average TikTok user

insights.claim: The rise of AI companionship and synthetic intimacy — chatbot friend, therapist, girlfriend, always-available listener — makes the Luddites' insistence on embodied unoptimized encounter politically charged, with the warning that a society organized around frictionless synthetic responsiveness could lose the muscles required for reciprocal life.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Flags AI companionship as the next front of cultural backlash after social media — a reputational and regulatory risk vector for consumer AI products.
insights.locator: But the explosion of screen-mediated connection

insights.claim: Plante frames early platform exposure as formative of sexuality itself, describing scrolling at age twelve through a feed that was half girls his age in swimsuits and half Yankees baseball players, with implications for how a generation understands itself and approaches others.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The developmental-harm argument is where platform liability litigation and age-verification legislation concentrate — this is the testimony that fuels it.
insights.quote: Tech had an “outsized effect on us as sexual beings in the world,”
insights.locator: Tech had an “outsized effect on us as sexual beings

insights.claim: Organizers deliberately resist framing tech resistance as addiction because they do not want a latter-day temperance movement, preferring a feminist consciousness-raising analogy, while the author counters that the hallmark of addiction is precisely choicelessness and that dominant technologies were engineered for maximum dependence for reasons of profit.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The addiction frame is the one that historically produces product-liability and design regulation; movement leaders avoiding it is a reason platform legal risk from this quarter stays muted.
insights.locator: I did ask them about tech addiction

insights.claim: Anti-Big-Tech sentiment is currently multipartisan with adherents on right and left, with data center protests lighting up the country and Gallup finding in 2026 that seven in ten Americans opposed an AI data center being built in their local area.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: A 70 percent local-opposition rate is a direct siting and permitting risk to the AI capex buildout — the most tradeable datapoint in the piece.
insights.quote: In 2026, Gallup found that seven in ten Americans opposed an AI data center being built in their local area.
insights.locator: For the moment, anti-Big-Tech sentiment is multipartisan

insights.claim: The coalition already spans JD Vance praising Lina Khan's antitrust approach and supporting checks on Big Tech so smaller firms can compete, and a guest pastor in small-town Illinois preaching about social media as a kind of sin.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Bipartisan elite plus grassroots religious hostility means platform regulation has no natural partisan defender — a durable overhang on Big Tech policy risk.
insights.locator: JD Vance has praised Lina Khan’s antitrust approach

insights.claim: The Luddites' ideological openness and low barrier to entry is both a resocialization strategy against algorithmic sectarianism and a strategic necessity, because they face AI companies with eye-watering investments and tech corporations increasingly fused with and financially backed by governments — making true mass politics possibly the only viable route.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Explicitly names state-corporate fusion in AI as the asymmetry — the same fusion that underwrites the capex cycle also insulates it from ordinary political challenge.
insights.locator: They and other anti-tech groups are up against titanic forces

insights.claim: The author flags unresolved risks to the movement's growth, including access for the time-poor, socially anxious or disabled, and who gets welcomed or sidelined as it matures.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: In-person-only organizing has a structural ceiling — the people most captured by screens may be the least able to attend, capping conversion.
insights.locator: In ways that coexisted with being moved by their organizing

themes.theme: The author's ambivalence and the physical internet

insights.claim: The author argues social media genuinely enabled marriage equality, the Arab Spring, Black Lives Matter, mutual aid networks and disabled communities, but that many of those shifts in mass opinion were easy-come easy-go — mercurial, shallowly held and easily co-opted — as the current reactionary backlash shows.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: A rare steelman-then-discount of platform social value: the gains were real but not durable, which weakens the industry's main defense against regulation.
insights.locator: Social media platforms, in my lifetime, helped ordinary people

insights.claim: The spectral online world has physically terraformed the planet through undersea cables spanning continents, data centers the size of Manhattan, child laborers in cobalt mine shafts, satellites, server farms, water, electricity, logistics and militarized supply chains — framed by Bogna Konior as one of the greatest terraforming projects our species has undertaken.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The physical-footprint framing is the bridge between cultural tech criticism and concrete resource fights over land, water and power for data centers.
insights.locator: The online world presents itself as spectral

insights.claim: Anton Barba-Kay's argument, cited approvingly, is that the internet operates the way heaven and hell did for Christians of old — a place entered daily by imagination and desire that we make real by behaving as if it were real, transformatively reprogramming how we think and act.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: A model of platform power as belief-constituted rather than technologically determined, implying norms can dissolve engagement faster than features can hold it.
insights.locator: She goes on to reference the philosopher Anton Barba-Kay

insights.claim: Mark Fisher's debtor-addict as late capitalism's ideal subject — bound by need and compulsion, disciplined through private shame — is used to argue that the choicelessness around technology feels structural rather than personal, with Big Tech dominance framed to the public as inevitable.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Reframing inevitability as manufactured is the movement's core persuasion move; if it lands, perceived switching costs fall.
insights.locator: Mark Fisher wrote of the debtor-addict

insights.claim: The author's own capture was severe enough to be hidden in a way alcohol could not be — she read article after article and was hypnotized by YouTube during a depression, and shocked a friend when she disclosed her actual screentime — while a single Luddite event left her not looking at her phone for six hours.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: The invisibility of heavy phone use relative to substance use is why the harm has no social enforcement mechanism — and why norm-setting events have outsized effect.
insights.quote: If I had taken to drinking, my loved ones would have noticed in weeks.
insights.locator: Having loved addicts, I’ve always been mindful

insights.claim: The report ends with a Luddite organizer asking the author to put her phone away while she filmed the movement's own play, saying 'We don't do that here' — norm enforcement, not technology refusal, is what the movement actually produces.
insights.speaker: N+1 Magazine
insights.so_what: Social sanction against filming and scrolling in shared space is the mechanism most likely to dent engagement at scale — watch for it spreading to venues, restaurants and workplaces.
insights.quote: “Could you put that away?” she asked, mild irritation in her face. “We don’t do that here.”
insights.locator: Someone tapped me on the shoulder
